meta.title: GLP-1 Agonists Are Associated With a Significant Reduction in Breast Cancer Incidence in Women.
meta.abstract:
Purpose

Excess weight is a key modifiable risk factor for breast cancer. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1) promote weight loss and improve metabolic health, but their effect on breast cancer risk remains unclear.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study from January 1, 2022, to June 30, 2025, using electronic health records. We identified 217,624 unique women who underwent breast imaging; restricting to ages 45-80 years with a BMI ≥25 and a documented imaging outcome (n = 111,646; median age 61 years). The primary outcome was breast cancer detection. GLP-1 use was defined as a first prescription before the examination date and assessed in relation to race, ethnicity, age, and type 2 diabetes. To address potential confounding between these covariates and GLP-1 exposure, we performed one-to-one, case-control matching using propensity scores on the basis of age, race, ethnicity, highest BMI, breast density, and history of type 2 diabetes. The propensity matching to the GLP-1 use group was performed using the greedy nearest neighbor approach.

Results

GLP-1 exposure was associated with a lower incidence of breast cancer (odds ratio [OR], 0.649 [95% CI, 0.569 to 0.741]; P < .0001). In the matched logistic regression (30,528 observations; 600 cancer cases), GLP-1 exposure was associated with a lower breast cancer incidence (OR, 0.695 [95% CI, 0.590 to 0.819]; P < .0001).

Conclusion

In this large observational study of women undergoing breast imaging at a major academic center and affiliated sites, GLP-1 treatment was associated with a lower incidence of breast cancer, independent of age, race, ethnicity, BMI, breast density, and diabetes. The findings support the need for prospective trials investigating GLP-1 agonists for breast cancer prevention.

domains.name: Selection of participants into the study
domains.direction_justification: Conditioning cohort inclusion on undergoing breast imaging during the study period (n = 217,624) creates collider stratification bias: GLP-1 users who undergo routine screening are subject to healthy-user healthcare utilization patterns, whereas non-users undergoing imaging may be enriched for diagnostic indications (symptomatic workup) with higher baseline cancer yield (2.47% vs 1.62%; Table 1).

findings.title: Selection conditioned on breast imaging encounter
findings.mechanism: Restricting the cohort to patients with documented breast imaging outcomes induces selection bias because reasons for imaging (screening vs diagnostic evaluation of a palpable mass) differ systematically between actively managed GLP-1 users and controls.
evidence: We identified 217,624 unique women who underwent breast imaging; restricting to ages 45-80 years with a BMI >= 25 and a documented imaging outcome (n = 111,646)

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: Primary outcome was confirmed via malignant breast pathology diagnoses in the health system EHR, which provides objective histologic confirmation.

findings.title: Objective histopathology ascertainment
findings.mechanism: Outcome detection relied on standardized histologic pathology records of malignancy, minimizing outcome misclassification.
evidence: The primary outcome was a malignant breast pathology diagnosis during the study period (Methods, page 2)

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: No prospective study protocol or pre-registered statistical analysis plan was cited, and only simple unadjusted and propensity score-matched logistic regressions were presented without time-to-event Cox models accounting for censoring or exposure duration.

findings.title: Absence of time-to-event modeling
findings.mechanism: Binary logistic regression ignores differences in follow-up time, timing of GLP-1 initiation, and interval to cancer diagnosis.
evidence: a logistic regression model was performed on the matched data set, with GLP-1 agonist use as the only covariate of interest (Methods, page 2)

overall.summary: This retrospective EHR study reports an odds ratio of 0.695 (95% CI, 0.590 to 0.819) for breast cancer associated with GLP-1 agonist use in matched overweight/obese women undergoing breast imaging. However, the study suffers from high risk of bias in confounding, exposure classification, and participant selection. Exposure was defined as any single prescription before the imaging date without requiring a biologically plausible latency window, duration of use, or adherence verification. Furthermore, restricting the study sample to patients receiving breast imaging introduces collider/selection bias, and unmeasured confounders (including parity, family history, and residual prior breast cancer history) strongly bias the observed association away from the null.
